sentences.text: The *Marged Ann* went out at ten past six with two aboard and did not come back.
Merryn was fourteen.
It was a flat grey day with no weather in it whatsoever, which matters, and the other ten boats were in by half past two.
She has checked the record.
Wind at the Lizard that afternoon was force two to three, visibility good, sea slight.
It is the single data point in the whole of her life that her own explanation does not cover, and she has been extremely careful never to build anything on it.
By four the harbour knew.

By five the coastguard had it and there was a lifeboat out of Falmouth and two of the crabbers had gone back out, and by seven it was dark and there was a helicopter working the ground west of the Manacles.
Merryn was at her grandmother's, which is where the family goes.
There is a particular thing that happens in a village on an evening like that and it is not what people imagine.
Nobody stood on the wall.
Nobody wailed.
Merryn's cousin, who was seventeen, did the sandwiches.
That is what he did for eleven hours: he made sandwiches for people who were not eating, and put them on the table, and took them away, and made more, and nobody told him to and nobody stopped him.
Merryn has thought about that as much as she has thought about the bird.
What there was, for eleven hours, was a kitchen with too many people in it and a great deal of tea and long stretches of ordinary conversation that stopped every time a phone went.
At about nine her grandmother got up and went to the window and stood there for a while.
She was seventy-eight and she had buried a brother off that coast in 1969 and she had not said a word for two hours.
Merryn asked her what she was doing.

Her grandmother said: "She's on the post." And Merryn, who had done fifty-eight days with a notebook two years earlier and knew exactly what she thought about all of it, went and stood at that window and looked down the harbour at a post in the dark with a bird-shaped thing on it and did not say one word about confirmation bias.
They found the *Marged Ann* at twenty to two in the morning, eleven miles south-south-west, with a fouled prop and a dead radio and two extremely cold and extremely embarrassed men aboard.
The prop had picked up a length of somebody else's rope, which happens perhaps twice a year in that fleet and is normally a nuisance and an hour with a knife.
The radio had failed for a reason that was never satisfactorily established and that one of the two men was extremely defensive about for the next decade.
Nobody was hurt.
